clue.text: Old man's furry creature exhibited in fair

parts.note: the old man is a familiar name for one's father, PA, here with the possessive S
the sable is a small weasel-like animal prized for its fur

explanation.surface: Someone's father shows off a fur-bearing animal at the county fair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exhibited in' is just a link joining the wordplay to the definition; 'fair' is the adjective meaning middling, not the funfair the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair in the sense of tolerable or adequate is a synonym: work that is just about acceptable.

clue.text: Impractical piece of furniture

explanation.surface: A chair or sofa is judged to be not much use.
explanation.definitionFit: An armchair critic theorises without practical experience, so the word as adjective means unpractical; it is also an upholstered seat with side rests.

clue.text: What's good enough 'e extracted from French composer's works

indicators.note: something extracted from a word is drawn out of it, so the letter is removed from the composer's name

parts.note: Erik Satie was a French composer; with the possessive S his name gives these letters
written as printed, the letter e with an apostrophe as if a dropped h
a works is a factory, a plant where things are made

explanation.surface: A Cockney 'e' is lifted out of some piece of music by a French composer, leaving something acceptable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'works' poses as the composer's output, but it means a plant or mill. The apostrophe in 'e mimics a dropped h and is surface dressing; only the letter counts.
explanation.definitionFit: Something adequate is good enough, meeting the required standard without excelling.

clue.text: Old fortress in Elba still exists

indicators.note: the answer lies in the run of letters spanning these three clue words

explanation.surface: An ancient castle is said to survive on Elba, Napoleon's island of exile.
explanation.walkthrough: The run spans elBA STILL Exists.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bastille was the Paris fortress and prison stormed in 1789, a historic stronghold.

clue.text: Mission my base's ordered

indicators.note: ordered here means arranged differently, so these letters are put into a new order

parts.note: the word base's taken with its S as a letter of the fodder

explanation.surface: A military mission is commanded by a person's home base.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive S of base's counts as a letter here: MY BASES rearranged gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A diplomatic mission is a synonym for the ambassador's official residence and staff abroad.

clue.text: Huntsman never the same again?

explanation.surface: A hunter worries that life will never be the same after this.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is cryptic: a drink taken after another is of a different kind, so it is never the same drink again.
explanation.definitionFit: A huntsman is one who pursues quarry; a whisky after beer, or beer after whisky, is a follow-up drink of a different sort.

clue.text: Right time for fashion

parts.note: an age is a long period of time

explanation.surface: The correct moment for some fashion trend.
explanation.definitionFit: Something all the rage is in fashion; the craze or vogue of the moment.

clue.text: Showy white flower I left out in wind

indicators.note: left out means the letters are omitted from the flower's name

parts.note: the Easter lily is a showy white trumpet lily

explanation.surface: A showy white bloom is missed out of the arrangement, blowing in the breeze.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking IL out of EASTER LILY leaves the answer. 'in' is a link word before the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A wind blowing from the east is named by its direction, used as a noun.

clue.text: Prince's turn for a drink with an actor

definitions.note: the 's stands for is: the prince is what the wordplay builds

indicators.note: turn here means the combined letters are read backwards

parts.note: a jar is British slang for a drink, especially of beer
a ham is a bad, overacting performer

explanation.surface: A royal takes a turn and has a pint with a theatrical performer.
explanation.walkthrough: One reversal turns the whole string A JAR A HAM end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: A maharaja is an Indian ruling prince, the title meaning great king.

clue.text: What's obscene must corrupt

indicators.note: corrupt as a verb means to spoil or alter, so these four letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Indecent material is bound to corrupt people.
explanation.definitionFit: Smut is obscene talk or pictures, indecent material.

clue.text: Hard to convert information while being conveyed outside

indicators.note: being conveyed outside means the phrase for travelling goes around the other piece

parts.note: goods in transit are on their way, being carried
gen is British slang for information

explanation.surface: Someone resists conversion while hearing information carried outdoors.
explanation.walkthrough: GEN goes inside IN TRANSIT, between its last two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An obstinate person refuses to be persuaded, so is hard to convert to another view.

clue.text: Responsibility for minor daily transport

parts.note: The Guardian is a British daily newspaper
a ship transports goods; to ship is to transport

explanation.surface: Who is responsible for delivering a small daily paper?
explanation.definitionFit: A legal guardian has custody of a child, the duty of care for someone under age.

clue.text: It's not wrong to give pounds to very poor

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for pounds sterling, from the Latin libra
awful means very bad, of terrible quality

explanation.surface: Giving money to the destitute is no sin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'very poor' looks like the needy, but it is the adjective for dreadful quality.
explanation.definitionFit: Something legal is permitted, so it is not wrong in the eyes of the law.

clue.text: Flag-ship rounds end of pier

indicators.note: rounds means goes around, so the vessel encloses the letter

parts.note: a steamer is a ship driven by steam

indicators.note: end of picks the last letter of the word pier

explanation.surface: The leading vessel of a fleet sails round the tip of a jetty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flag-ship' reads as one word but splits: Flag is the definition, ship the wordplay. R goes inside STEAMER.
explanation.definitionFit: A long narrow pennant or banner flying from a mast is a kind of flag.

clue.text: Superb specimen takes the biscuit

explanation.surface: An excellent example is the best of all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes the biscuit' is an idiom for being the most outrageous, but here 'takes' is a link and the biscuit is a definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A cracker is British slang for an outstanding example of something; it is also a thin crisp unsweetened biscuit.

clue.text: Wine found in many picnic baskets

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, hence many
hampers are large wicker baskets for carrying a picnic

explanation.surface: Bottles of wine are packed in many picnic baskets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found in' is just a link. CHAMPERS is British slang for champagne.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for champagne, the sparkling French wine.

clue.text: It's not clear how days should be organized

indicators.note: organized means set in order, so these seven letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A planner is unsure how the days ought to be scheduled.
explanation.definitionFit: Something shadowy is dim and indistinct, so vague and not clear.

clue.text: Scope for capital growth

parts.note: reads like investment jargon, but capital is the head and the scope is space overhead for it

explanation.surface: An investment offers potential for money to grow.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital (from Latin caput) is the head; room above it is the clearance in a car or doorway.
explanation.definitionFit: Clearance above someone's head, figuratively any margin or leeway.

clue.text: Aware the cuckoo is a bird…

indicators.note: cuckoo means crazy, signalling that the letters of these words go haywire

explanation.surface: One who knows the cuckoo is a bird states the obvious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cuckoo' poses as the bird, but it is the anagram signal; the answer is another bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The wheatear is a small migratory songbird of the thrush family with a white rump.

clue.text: … and this one's yellow

parts.note: continues the previous clue: another bird, and yellow in the slang sense of cowardly

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links back to the bird of 18 down, so this one is a bird too, with yellow meaning lacking courage.
explanation.definitionFit: A farmyard fowl, and slang for a coward, someone yellow-bellied.

clue.text: Physician gets completely round the course

parts.note: all means wholly, as in all gone
O is round in shape
a path is a course or track taken

explanation.surface: A doctor jogs around the whole track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets' is a link word. An allopath is a practitioner of conventional medicine, as opposed to homeopathy.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctor who treats illness with drugs producing opposite effects, i.e. a conventional medical practitioner.

clue.text: For this Latin verse I need a translation

indicators.note: translation means turning into another form, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A student needs a crib to read this Latin poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' is a link word. The anagram fodder is I NEED A.
explanation.definitionFit: Virgil's epic poem about Aeneas, written in Latin hexameters.

clue.text: Surprised a maiden with a final letter

parts.note: M is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for a maiden over, one with no runs
zed is the British name for Z, the last letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: A young woman is astonished to receive a last letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' is just a link. In cricket a maiden is an over in which no runs are scored.
explanation.definitionFit: Astonished, struck with wonder: a synonym.

clue.text: Deckhand has two sets of these

definitions.text: Deckhand has two sets of these

parts.words: Deckhand has two sets of these
parts.note: split the sailor's word into deck and hand: both are groups of the same items used in games

explanation.surface: A sailor has two of something on board.
explanation.walkthrough: A deck is the full pack and a hand is what one player holds.
explanation.definitionFit: Cards used for games like bridge and poker, dealt from a pack.

clue.text: A manner or expression that's dismissive

parts.note: way means manner, as in a way of speaking

explanation.surface: A gesture or remark that brushes someone off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'or' is a link word between wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Shouted as an interjection, it means go, be off with you, telling someone to leave.

clue.text: Unpleasant character's inclination

explanation.surface: A nasty person's tendency.
explanation.walkthrough: 's is a link word. A ship heels when it leans to one side.
explanation.definitionFit: A cad or scoundrel is a contemptible person; a ship's list or tilt to one side is a lean.

clue.text: By the way, this is an attack without a leader

indicators.note: without a leader means the first letter of the word for an attack is dropped

parts.note: a broadside is a fierce attack, originally all the guns on one side of a ship firing together

explanation.surface: Incidentally, this is an assault with nobody in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By the way' poses as the aside 'incidentally', but it is the definition, meaning beside the road.
explanation.definitionFit: The verge beside a highway is literally by the way, way meaning road.

clue.text: Romeo, for example, getting call to go

parts.note: to call someone something is to name them
to part is to leave, go away

explanation.surface: Romeo hears someone calling him to leave Juliet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting' is a link word. A name-part is a title role, the character a play is named after.
explanation.definitionFit: A title role in a play, like Shakespeare's lover in Romeo and Juliet.
